kf1.tip: Pick a sport you play. Name one action using a ball-and-socket joint (hip or shoulder) and one using a hinge joint (elbow, knee or ankle), with the bones at each.
kf1.note: A good answer names a real action, the joint type and every bone at that joint. Kicking a football is a clear example. The femur swings at the hip, a ball-and-socket joint made by the pelvis and femur. The tibia swings at the knee, a hinge joint made by the femur and tibia. Check your pairings. The shoulder is the scapula and humerus. The elbow is the humerus, radius and ulna. The ankle is the tibia, fibula and talus.

kf2.tip: Rank support, protection, mineral storage and blood cell production by how much they matter to a rugby player during a match, and defend each place in a line.
kf2.note: A strong answer links each function to something that happens in the match. Most would put protection or support first. The ribcage absorbs tackle impacts that would otherwise damage the heart and lungs, and the skeleton holds up the player's body weight. Blood cell production comes next, because red blood cells carry oxygen to working muscles. Mineral storage usually comes last, because bones gain mineral density over time, not within one game. The trap is ranking without giving a rugby reason.

cs1.tip: Imagine the end of the humerus were rounded like the head of the femur, not pulley-shaped. Say what would change at the elbow during a bicep curl.
cs1.note: The key point is that bone shape decides how much movement a joint allows. The pulley-shaped end of the humerus sits in the groove of the ulna, which limits the elbow to flexion and extension in one plane. A rounded end would act like the femur at the hip and allow movement in all directions. The curl would still bend and straighten, but the forearm would no longer be held to one path. A weaker answer confuses this with the radius turning around the ulna.
